issues.legal_issue: A court must judicially decide an objection to a document’s admissibility when it is tendered, and merely marking the document subject to objection does not make its admission final.
material_facts: An objection that the document was insufficiently stamped and unregistered was raised when it was tendered in evidence.

The trial court marked the document subject to objection without deciding the objection, and rejected it only later by relying on the rule that an admitted document cannot subsequently be challenged for insufficient stamping.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was required to decide the objection judicially before marking the document as an exhibit. Because it had only tentatively marked the document and had not judicially determined admissibility, the bar against a later challenge did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 35 and 36 of the Stamp Act, the protection against a later challenge applies where the court has judicially admitted the document; a tentative marking subject to objection is not such an admission. The court must determine the objection when the document is tendered and before it is marked. The Court relied on Javar Chand v. Pukhraj Surana, AIR 1961 SC 1655.

predicates.civil_trial_document_admissibility_dispu: A document is tendered as evidence in a civil trial and its admissibility is disputed.
predicates.objection_raised_when_document_tendered: A party objects to the document’s admissibility when it is tendered in evidence.
predicates.court_deferred_decision_by_tentative_mar: The court marks the document subject to objection without judicially deciding its admissibility at that time.

issues.definition: When a document is disputed in a civil trial and the court only marks it tentatively after an objection, that marking does not make its admission final.

issues.legal_issue: A chargeable instrument that is not duly stamped must be impounded and cannot be admitted in evidence until the required duty and penalty are paid.
material_facts: The document was found not to be duly stamped.
The party tendering it had not paid the required duty or penalty.
issues.conclusion: The instrument had to be impounded and dealt with according to law, and it was inadmissible in evidence while the required duty and penalty remained unpaid.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 33 and 35 of the Stamp Act require a court authorized to receive evidence to impound a chargeable instrument found not duly stamped and prohibit its admission in evidence until the required duty and penalty are paid. Section 36 does not prevent this result where the document was only tentatively marked and its admissibility was not judicially determined.

rule.if: civil_trial_evidence_proceeding and chargeable_instrument_not_duly_stamped and instrument_produced_to_evidence_receiving_court and required_duty_and_penalty_unpaid

predicates.civil_trial_evidence_proceeding: A party seeks to rely on a document as evidence in a civil trial.
predicates.chargeable_instrument_not_duly_stamped: The document is chargeable with stamp duty but is not duly stamped.
predicates.instrument_produced_to_evidence_receivin: The document is produced to a court authorized to receive evidence.
predicates.required_duty_and_penalty_unpaid: The required duty and penalty have not been paid.

issues.definition: When a chargeable instrument produced as evidence in a civil trial is not duly stamped and the required duty and penalty are unpaid, it must be impounded and excluded until they are paid.

issues.legal_issue: A hereditary Shebait office enjoyed by turns is immovable property, so a gift transferring that office requires a registered instrument.
material_facts: The right to worship by turn carried the office of Shebait, including the right during the holder’s turn to officiate and receive offerings.
The office was hereditary, and the document purported to transfer it in the present as a gift.
The gift instrument was unregistered and was relied on to establish the claimed transfer.
issues.conclusion: The hereditary office enjoyed by turn was immovable property, and the unregistered gift instrument was inadmissible to establish its transfer.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 2(6) of the Registration Act, whose definition of immovable property includes hereditary allowances, and the requirement that a gift of immovable property be made by registered instrument. It treated the office and property interests in Shebaitship as inseparable. It relied on Angurbala Mullick v. Debabrata Mullick, [1951] SCR 1125, and Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] SCR 1005, and approved the earlier authorities recognizing hereditary religious offices as immovable property.

rule.if: civil_gift_transfer_dispute and hereditary_religious_office_enjoyed_by_turn and gift_purports_to_transfer_the_office and gift_instrument_unregistered

predicates.civil_gift_transfer_dispute: A party relies on a gift instrument in a civil proceeding to establish a transfer of property.
predicates.hereditary_religious_office_enjoyed_by_t: The property at issue is a hereditary religious office that its holder enjoys by turns.
predicates.gift_purports_to_transfer_the_office: The instrument purports to transfer the office by gift.
predicates.gift_instrument_unregistered: The instrument purporting to make the gift is not registered.

issues.definition: When an unregistered gift instrument purports to transfer a hereditary religious office enjoyed by turns, it is inadmissible to establish that transfer.
